newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Fund buying drives ringgit to 17-month high.
newsitem.headline: Fund buying drives ringgit to 17-month high.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit extended a rally to hit a 17-month high on Monday, supported by brisk buying by U.S. and Japanese funds looking for capital gains and higher interest rates, dealers and analysts said.
In Asian trading, the ringgit strengthened to 2.4690 against the dollar before retreating to 2.4710 around midday on profit-taking and fears of intervention by the central Bank Negara.
Interbank dealers said Bank Negara had intervened at around 2.4780/90 to the dollar last Friday to slow the rise of the ringgit. No confirmation was available from the central bank.
The ringgit last traded below the 2.4700 level on August 15, 1995, when it touched an intraday high of 2.4620 a dollar. On December 31, 1996, the Malaysian unit closed at 2.5250 a dollar.
Most dealers and analysts said the ringgit was expected to gain further, with many talking about a run to 2.45 to the dollar in the next few days.
However, fears of a sharp retreat on speculative selling and Bank Negara intervention will slow movement both ways, they added.
Lum Chee Soon, general manager with PhileoAllied Securities in Kuala Lumpur, said the 2.18 percent appreciation in the ringgit this year was largely due to speculative buying.
"In the long run we were expecting the ringgit to touch this level, but not so fast. We really feel this is a short-term aberration," he said.
Lum said the run-up in the ringgit followed forecasts of a heavy flow of funds into the region in 1997.
A survey of banks by research firm IDEA, released on January 7, said the ringgit would be the favourite currency in the region.
Jimmy Koh, economist with IDEA, said on Monday that apart from an improvement in Malaysia's economic fundamentals, the sluggish Thai baht and Indonesian rupiah have aided the ringgit.
"Funds are coming in for yield play as well as for potential capital gains," he said.
An improvement in the country's trade balance and a slowdown in the fast-paced economic growth were the two main factors that triggered the recovery of the ringgit, Koh said.
He said weaker fundamentals in the Thai economy and Indonesia's intervention band restrictions were attracting most investors to the Malaysian currency.
Interest rate differentials also favour Malaysia. The benchmark three-month interbank rate in Kuala Lumpur, for example, is over four percentage points higher than in Singapore.
Malaysia's growing current account deficit and inflation raised fears last year about an overheating in the economy, forcing the country to keep interest rates high to slow growth.
Malaysia has recorded a sharply lower trade deficit of 954.35 million ringgit ($378.7 million) in the first 10 months of 1996 against around 9.96 billion in the corresponding period last year.

Malaysia's 1996 annual gross domestic product growth is expected to slow to 8.2 percent following 9.5 percent growth in 1995. The country has reported nine straight years of growth of over eight percent, a trend which is expected to be maintained until the year 2000.
